topic: Forces and motion: Forces and braking
subject: physics

items.q: A driver sees a hazard ahead and brings the car safely to rest. What is the stopping distance of the car?
items.correct: The thinking distance added to the braking distance.
items.misconception: The distance travelled once the brakes are applied.
items.why: In everyday speech 'stopping' begins when the brakes go on. The thinking phase feels like nothing is happening, even though the car is covering ground at full speed. The specification defines stopping distance as the sum of the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time and the distance travelled under the braking force. At 30 mph the thinking part is about 9 m of the 23 m total - well over a third.
items.random_wrong: Twice the thinking distance, as the two parts match.

items.q: A car is driven faster along the same road, and the braking force the brakes can produce is unchanged. What happens to the stopping distance?
items.correct: It rises: both the thinking and braking distances grow.
items.misconception: Only the braking distance grows; thinking distance is fixed.
items.why: The phrase 'thinking distance' invites students to treat it as a property of the driver. Reaction time genuinely is a property of the driver and does not change with speed, and students then attach that fixed-ness to the distance as well. The reaction time is fixed, but the car keeps moving at its full speed throughout that time. Distance = speed x time, so at twice the speed the car covers twice as much road in the same reaction time.
items.random_wrong: Only the thinking distance grows; braking distance is fixed.

items.q: A driver with a reaction time of 0.70 s is driving at 20 m/s when a hazard appears. What is the thinking distance?
items.why: In the familiar Highway Code table the 20 mph row shows 6 m and 6 m, and that first row is the one students remember. It is the only row in which the two are equal. Thinking distance grows in proportion to speed while braking distance grows with speed squared, so they separate quickly. At 70 mph the figures are about 21 m thinking and 75 m braking.

items.q: A car's speed doubles from 15 m/s to 30 m/s. The driver's reaction time and the braking force are unchanged. What happens to the two parts of the stopping distance?
items.correct: Thinking distance doubles; braking distance rises about four times.
items.misconception: Thinking distance doubles and the braking distance is unchanged.
items.why: Students correctly learn that a bigger braking force gives a shorter stop, then treat the braking force as the only variable and forget that it has to remove a quantity of kinetic energy that depends on speed. The brakes must do work equal to the vehicle's kinetic energy. With the force fixed, a faster vehicle has more kinetic energy to remove, so the brakes must act over a longer distance.
items.random_wrong: Thinking distance is unchanged and the braking distance doubles.

items.q: Stopping distance is plotted on the vertical axis against speed on the horizontal axis for one car. What shape is the graph?
items.correct: A curve that gets steeper, as braking distance grows fastest.
items.misconception: A straight line from the origin, as distance follows speed.
items.why: Thinking distance really does double, so students apply the same proportional rule to the braking distance without checking it against data or against the energy argument. Braking force x braking distance = kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x speed squared. With the force fixed, doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy and so quadruples the braking distance. Typical data show this: at 30 mph the braking distance is about 14 m, at 60 mph about 55 m.
items.random_wrong: A horizontal line, because the braking force does not change.

items.q: Stopping distance against speed is plotted for a car and for a loaded lorry on the same axes. The lorry's line lies above the car's line at every speed. What does this show?
items.correct: At any given speed the lorry needs a longer distance to stop.
items.misconception: At any given speed the lorry comes to rest more quickly.
items.why: Students carry over an everyday reading of graphs in which 'higher is better', as with test scores or performance charts, instead of reading the y-axis label. Read the axis. The y-axis is a distance needed in order to stop, so a higher line means a longer, and therefore worse, stopping distance at that speed.
items.random_wrong: The lorry's heavy load makes its driver's reaction time longer.

items.q: Which range gives the typical values of human reaction time?
items.correct: 0.2 s to 0.9 s
items.misconception: 0.5 s to 1.5 s
items.why: One second is the round number students reach for, and the Highway Code figures happen to be based on a reaction time of about 0.7 s, which rounds up to 'about a second' in most retellings. Learn the specification's range: 0.2 s to 0.9 s, and expect real variation between people. Even within the range, the slowest driver's thinking distance is over four times the fastest driver's at the same speed.
items.random_wrong: 1.0 s to 3.0 s

items.q: Which of these would increase a driver's thinking distance at a given speed?
items.correct: The driver is tired at the end of a long shift.
items.misconception: The road ahead is covered with ice and slush.
items.why: Students know bad weather makes driving more dangerous overall, and attach that general danger to both parts of the stopping distance rather than asking which mechanism is affected. Ice reduces the grip between tyres and road, which affects how far the car travels once the brakes are on. The reaction time is a property of the driver, so the thinking distance at a given speed is unchanged.
items.random_wrong: The tyres are worn below the legal tread depth.

items.q: A ruler drop test is used to measure a student's reaction time. Which statement about the method is correct?
items.correct: The distance the ruler falls is measured and converted to a time.
items.misconception: The number of centimetres the ruler falls is the reaction time.
items.why: Some printed rulers used for the test have a time scale marked alongside the centimetre scale, so students remember reading a value off the ruler without noticing which scale it came from. The ruler measures a distance in centimetres, not a time in seconds. The ruler falls freely under gravity, so the fall distance is converted to a time using a chart or the free-fall relationship.
items.random_wrong: The catcher is told exactly when the ruler will be released.

items.q: A class measures reaction times using the ruler drop test. Which result is typical for a student?
items.correct: About 0.20 s
items.misconception: About 1.20 s
items.why: One second is the round number students reach for, and the Highway Code figures happen to be based on a reaction time of about 0.7 s, which rounds up to 'about a second' in most retellings. Learn the specification's range: 0.2 s to 0.9 s, and expect real variation between people. Even within the range, the slowest driver's thinking distance is over four times the fastest driver's at the same speed.
items.random_wrong: About 2.00 s

items.q: One student's five ruler drop results are 0.19 s, 0.21 s, 0.20 s, 0.55 s and 0.20 s. How should these results be treated?
items.correct: Treat 0.55 s as anomalous; take the mean of the other four.
items.misconception: Take the smallest value, as that is the true reaction time.
items.why: Reaction time feels like a personal best, and in sport the best performance is the one that counts. Students transfer that habit into the laboratory. A single quickest value may be a lucky anticipation rather than a genuine reaction. A mean of repeated readings, with clear anomalies excluded, is the more reliable estimate.
items.random_wrong: Take the mean of all five, as no result can be left out.

items.q: Data for one driver at 13 m/s show a thinking distance of 9 m when alert and 15 m after drinking alcohol. What do these data show?
items.correct: The alcohol has raised the reaction time by about 0.5 s.
items.misconception: The alcohol has raised the driver's reaction time by about 6.0 s.
items.why: Students subtract the two given numbers and carry the answer straight across to whatever quantity the question asks about, without checking units. Metres are not seconds. Divide each thinking distance by the speed to get a reaction time, then subtract. A 6 m increase at 13 m/s corresponds to an extra 0.46 s.
items.random_wrong: The alcohol has raised the braking distance by about 6 m.

items.q: Which of these increases the braking distance of a car?
items.correct: Rain has made the road surface wet and slippery.
items.misconception: The driver is tired at the end of a long trip.
items.why: Students picture a tired driver braking feebly and slowly, mixing the driver's alertness up with the force the brakes can generate. Braking distance is decided by the braking force, the speed, the road conditions and the state of brakes and tyres. Tiredness is one of the factors the specification lists as affecting reaction time, alongside drugs and alcohol.
items.random_wrong: The driver has taken a drug causing drowsiness.

items.q: Poor condition of a vehicle can increase its braking distance. Which pair of parts does this cover?
items.correct: The brakes and the tyres.
items.misconception: The brakes and the engine.
items.why: 'Poor condition of the vehicle' sounds like a description of the whole car, so students list every component they can think of rather than the two the specification names. The specification limits poor vehicle condition to the brakes or the tyres. Worn pads reduce the braking force; worn tyres reduce grip. The engine and gearbox drive the car forward and play no part in stopping it.
items.random_wrong: The brakes but not the tyres.

items.q: On an icy road, drivers are advised to leave a much bigger gap to the vehicle in front. Which statement best explains this advice?
items.correct: The ice lengthens the braking distance, so more space is needed.
items.misconception: The ice lengthens the driver's reaction time and thinking distance.
items.why: Students know bad weather makes driving more dangerous overall, and attach that general danger to both parts of the stopping distance rather than asking which mechanism is affected. Ice reduces the grip between tyres and road, which affects how far the car travels once the brakes are on. The reaction time is a property of the driver, so the thinking distance at a given speed is unchanged.
items.random_wrong: The ice stops the brakes from being able to grip the wheel.

items.q: A car is travelling at 27 m/s. The driver's reaction time is 0.70 s and the car decelerates at 6.5 m/s2 while braking. Estimate the stopping distance.
items.why: In everyday speech 'stopping' begins when the brakes go on. The thinking phase feels like nothing is happening, even though the car is covering ground at full speed. The specification defines stopping distance as the sum of the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time and the distance travelled under the braking force. At 30 mph the thinking part is about 9 m of the 23 m total - well over a third.

items.q: A car is slowed by applying its brakes. Which description of the energy transfer is correct?
items.correct: Work done by friction cuts the kinetic energy and heats the brakes.
items.misconception: Friction in the brakes destroys the kinetic energy of the car.
items.why: Friction is introduced as the force that 'takes energy away', and because the car ends up motionless the energy appears to have vanished with the motion. Energy cannot be destroyed, only transferred. The work done against friction raises the temperature of the brakes, and that thermal energy is then dissipated to the surroundings.
items.random_wrong: The brakes store the kinetic energy and return it later on.

items.q: A lorry brakes hard several times while descending a long hill. What happens to the temperature of its brakes?
items.correct: It rises, because work is done against friction at the brakes.
items.misconception: It falls, because the lorry is losing its kinetic energy.
items.why: 'Losing energy' is read as 'having less of everything', and students do not track where the energy goes as it is transferred out of the kinetic store. The vehicle loses kinetic energy, but that energy arrives somewhere: in the brakes. The specification is explicit that the temperature of the brakes increases.
items.random_wrong: It rises, but only because the engine is working hard.

items.q: Two identical cars must each be brought to rest in a braking distance of 30 m. One is travelling at 15 m/s, the other at 30 m/s. What can be said about the braking forces needed?
items.correct: The faster car needs the greater braking force.
items.misconception: Both need the same force; only the distance differs.
items.why: Students correctly learn that a bigger braking force gives a shorter stop, then treat the braking force as the only variable and forget that it has to remove a quantity of kinetic energy that depends on speed. The brakes must do work equal to the vehicle's kinetic energy. With the force fixed, a faster vehicle has more kinetic energy to remove, so the brakes must act over a longer distance.
items.random_wrong: The faster car needs a smaller, longer-lasting force.

items.q: A car of mass 1200 kg is travelling at 20 m/s and must stop in a braking distance of 40 m. The work done by the brakes equals the car's kinetic energy. What average braking force is needed?
items.why: The squared term feels like the important part of the equation, and a factor of one half looks decorative next to it. The 0.5 is part of the equation and halves the answer. Every braking force calculated from kinetic energy will be twice too large without it.

items.q: A driver presses the brake pedal harder, which increases the braking force on the car. What happens to the car's motion?
items.correct: Its deceleration rises, so it slows down more sharply.
items.misconception: Its deceleration falls, so it slows down more gently.
items.why: The minus sign is doing real work here: -8 m/s2 is a smaller number than -4 m/s2, and students who reason with the signed value conclude the deceleration has been reduced. Deceleration is the size of the negative acceleration. A larger braking force gives a more negative acceleration, which is a larger deceleration - the vehicle slows more sharply.
items.random_wrong: Its deceleration is unchanged; the brakes just act longer.

items.q: Which pair of effects are the dangers that a very large deceleration may lead to?
items.correct: The brakes may overheat and control may be lost.
items.misconception: The brakes may cool too fast and then seize up.
items.why: Students who remember only that braking changes the temperature of the brakes have a fifty-fifty chance of remembering the direction wrongly, and 'cooling' fits the idea of the car losing energy. Braking raises the temperature of the brakes. A large deceleration transfers energy quickly, so the brakes can overheat and become less effective, and the vehicle may skid and become impossible to steer.
items.random_wrong: The engine may overheat and the car may stall.

items.q: A lorry driver brakes hard again and again while descending a long, steep hill. Why is this dangerous?
items.correct: The brakes overheat and become less able to stop the lorry.
items.misconception: The engine overheats because it works against the brakes.
items.why: The engine is the obvious hot part of a vehicle in everyday experience, so any heating is attributed to it rather than to the work done against friction at the brakes. The temperature rise is produced at the brakes themselves by the work done against friction, and it is largest when the brakes have removed the most kinetic energy - which is why long descents and repeated hard stops overheat them.
items.random_wrong: The brakes cool so quickly that they seize onto the wheel.

items.q: (Higher Tier) A car of mass 1000 kg slows from 20 m/s to rest in a distance of 25 m. Use v2 - u2 = 2 a s to estimate the average braking force on the car.
items.why: The 2 sits between two symbols in a formula the student is copying rather than reading, and dropping it produces an answer that still looks reasonable. Substitute into v2 - u2 = 2 a s exactly as it is given on the equation sheet. The factor of 2 halves the acceleration, and here it is the difference between 16 m/s2 and 8 m/s2.

items.q: (Higher Tier) A car of mass 1200 kg makes an emergency stop from 13 m/s, coming to rest in 4.0 s. Estimate the average braking force on the car.
items.why: F = m a and p = m v look almost identical, and the velocity is the quantity actually printed in the question while the acceleration has to be worked out. Find the deceleration first, from a = change in velocity / time or from v2 - u2 = 2 a s, then substitute into resultant force = mass x acceleration.

items.q: A car has badly worn tyres and is carrying a heavy load. Does that lengthen the thinking distance?
items.correct: No. Thinking distance depends only on the driver's reaction time and the speed of the vehicle.
items.misconception: Anything that makes a car harder to stop must make the thinking distance longer as well.
items.why: Students learn a list of factors that increase stopping distance and do not sort it into the two separate parts, so every factor gets attached to both. Thinking distance = speed x reaction time. Worn tyres and heavy loads cannot change either of those, so they act on the braking distance only. Sort every factor into 'driver' (thinking) or 'road and vehicle' (braking).
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Could a driver have a reaction time of 0.02 s?
items.correct: No. Typical human reaction times range from 0.2 s to 0.9 s, ten to forty times longer than that.
items.misconception: Reacting feels instant, so the reaction time must be a tiny fraction of a second - a few hundredths.
items.why: The experience of reacting carries no sense of duration, and students confuse the speed of a nerve impulse with the whole see-decide-move sequence. The signal has to travel to the brain, be processed, and travel back to the muscles, which move a limb. Measured values in the ruler drop test are around 0.2 s, matching the bottom of the specification's range.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does it matter whether the catcher is counted down before the ruler is released?
items.correct: Yes. The ruler must be released without warning, or the catcher can anticipate the drop and the result is not a reaction time.
items.misconception: Saying 'three, two, one, go' just makes the test fairer, since everyone gets the same warning.
items.why: Students associate fair testing with treating everyone identically, and a countdown feels like the fairest possible start signal. The test measures the time to react to seeing the ruler move. A countdown lets the catcher predict the moment and close their fingers on the count instead, giving an impossibly short 'reaction time'. Keeping everything else the same is what makes the test fair.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Four results cluster near 0.20 s and one is 0.55 s. Should the 0.55 s go into the mean?
items.correct: No. It is anomalous - far outside the spread of the others - so it should be identified and left out of the mean.
items.misconception: You have to include every measurement you made; throwing one away is fixing the data.
items.why: Students are rightly taught not to discard inconvenient results, and cannot yet tell the difference between discarding data that disagrees with a prediction and excluding a reading that is clearly the product of a mistake. Anomalies are excluded because something went wrong in that trial - a fumble, a distraction - not because the value is inconvenient. State that the result was anomalous and why, then take the mean of the rest.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A driver has been drinking alcohol. Which part of the stopping distance is increased?
items.correct: The thinking distance. Alcohol lengthens the driver's reaction time; the braking distance is unaffected.
items.misconception: Alcohol and drugs make the whole car harder to stop, so the braking distance goes up.
items.why: Road safety campaigns say drink-driving means 'you cannot stop in time', and students turn that general warning into a statement about the brakes. Alcohol and drugs act on the driver, not on the vehicle. They lengthen the reaction time and therefore the thinking distance. Braking distance is changed by the road, the weather and the vehicle's brakes and tyres.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do worn tyres affect a vehicle's braking distance?
items.correct: Yes. Tyres are named alongside brakes as the parts whose poor condition lengthens the braking distance.
items.misconception: Tyres are about grip and cornering; it is the brakes that stop the car, so only the brakes matter.
items.why: The word 'brakes' is in 'braking distance', which makes the brakes look like the only relevant component, and the role of the tyres in transmitting that braking to the road is invisible. Poor condition of the vehicle is limited to the vehicle's brakes or tyres - both count. Tyres with too little tread cannot clear water or hold the road, so the vehicle travels further before stopping.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is the braking distance longer on an icy road?
items.correct: Because the ice reduces the grip between the tyres and the road, so the vehicle travels further before it comes to rest.
items.misconception: The ice gets into the brakes so the brakes cannot grip the wheel any more.
items.why: Students know the friction force in braking acts between the brakes and the wheel, and reasonably assume that any slippery condition must be attacking that same surface. Braking involves two separate frictional contacts: the brakes on the wheel, and the tyres on the road. Ice and water affect the tyre-road contact, so the wheels can lock or slip while the brakes themselves work normally.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do the brakes store the car's kinetic energy and give it back when the car sets off again?
items.correct: No. The energy is transferred to the thermal store of the brakes, raising their temperature, and is then dissipated to the surroundings.
items.misconception: The brakes hold on to the energy, like a stretched spring, and release it again when you accelerate.
items.why: Students meet elastic potential energy first, where storing and returning energy is exactly what happens, and generalise that reversible picture to every energy transfer. Friction transfers energy to thermal stores and spreads it out; that transfer is not reversible. Energy to accelerate the car again comes from its fuel or battery, not from the hot brakes.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two identical cars must stop in the same distance, one from 15 m/s and one from 30 m/s. Do they need the same braking force?
items.correct: No. The greater the speed of a vehicle the greater the braking force needed to stop it in a certain distance.
items.misconception: The brakes on a car always produce the same force; going faster just means they have to act for longer.
items.why: A brake feels like a fixed component with one setting, and students who have grasped that the same brakes are fitted to both cars conclude the force must therefore be the same. The braking force depends on how hard the brakes are applied, and it is set by what the stop demands: force x braking distance must equal the kinetic energy. Over the same distance, the faster car needs the larger force.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the kinetic energy of a 1200 kg car travelling at 20 m/s?
items.correct: 240 000 J, from kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x speed squared = 0.5 x 1200 x 20 x 20.
items.misconception: Kinetic energy is 0.5 x mass x speed, so it is 0.5 x 1200 x 20 = 12 000 J.
items.why: The equation is usually written as 0.5 m v2, and in a rushed calculation the small superscript 2 is the easiest part of it to lose. The speed is squared. Write the substitution out in full - 0.5 x 1200 x 20 x 20 - so the square cannot be dropped. It is the squaring that makes braking distance grow so steeply with speed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A car's kinetic energy is 240 000 J and it stops in 40 m. What braking force was needed?
items.correct: 6000 N. Work done = force x distance, so force = 240 000 / 40 = 6000 N.
items.misconception: The energy is 240 000, so the force is 240 000 N - it is the same number, just written differently.
items.why: Energy and force are both 'how strong the effect is' in everyday language, and once a big number has been calculated students are reluctant to believe another step is needed. Joules and newtons are different quantities. Work done = force x distance, so the energy must be divided by the distance over which the force acts to give the force in newtons.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A car slows from 20 m/s to rest over 25 m. Is the deceleration 20/25 = 0.8 m/s2?
items.correct: No. Acceleration is a change in velocity divided by a time, or found from v2 - u2 = 2 a s; here it is 8 m/s2.
items.misconception: Acceleration is speed divided by distance, so dividing 20 by 25 gives it.
items.why: Students remember that acceleration is 'speed divided by something' and reach for whichever other number the question supplies - here a distance rather than a time. Check the units. Velocity divided by distance gives 1/s, not m/s2. Use acceleration = change in velocity / time taken when a time is given, and v2 - u2 = 2 a s when a distance is given.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A 1200 kg car stops in 4.0 s. Is the braking force 1200 x 4.0 = 4800 N?
items.correct: No. F = m a needs the acceleration, not the time. Here a = 13/4.0 = 3.25 m/s2, so the force is about 3900 N.
items.misconception: In F = m a you can put the time in for a if you have not worked the acceleration out.
items.why: Acceleration and time are both about how the motion changes over the stop, and under exam pressure students substitute the number they already have rather than doing the extra step. Work out the acceleration first: change in velocity divided by time taken. Only then substitute into F = m a. Checking units catches this - kg x s is not a newton.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
